ColoringIsotopy.summaryHtml: The surprise: this relation has no 'reverse' rule. It is a one-way street of moves along which colorings are proved to carry over, which is exactly what limits the invariance theorem.
ColoringIsotopy.bodyHtml:
Plain English

Definition (ColoringIsotopy, Flype.lean lines 216-265). The relation generated, in one direction, by:

  • reflexivity and transitivity (no symmetry);
  • Reidemeister I and II on well-formed diagrams, and a local model of Reidemeister III (IsReidemeisterIIILocal);
  • local flypes (IsLocalFlype) and planar isotopy (PlanarIsotopy);
  • add/mul congruences (the right-hand ones with a port side-condition);
  • reindexing identities: T + [0] → T, T → [0] + T, [±1] ↔ [±1]ⁱ, associativity both ways.

It leaves out the Figure 5 slides, half-turns, mirror and general inversion moves, and transfer moves. The repo shows that carrying a coloring with fixed boundary colors from a diagram to its mirror or inverse can fail (not_coloring_mirror_transport, not_coloring_invert_transport).

coloring_fraction_ColoringIsotopy proves that every coloring can be carried along any ColoringIsotopy path with the same boundary colors.
caveatsHtml: No lemma in the repo proves WellFormed for any construction, so the R1/R2 moves are usable only where a caller supplies it (Claude audit, §4).

Crossing.summaryHtml: The surprise: a crossing is just four numbers read counterclockwise, with the over-strand on ports 0 and 2. The coloring rule only ever looks at which port an arc sits on.
Crossing.bodyHtml:
Plain English

Definition (Crossing, Reidemeister.lean lines 71-81). A crossing has arc numbers a0, a1, a2, a3 at its four ports, read counterclockwise. Ports 0 and 2 belong to the over-strand, ports 1 and 3 to the two pieces of the under-strand. It also has a sign: pos as in [+1], neg as in [−1].

Because the over-strand occupies ports 0 and 2, the coloring rule (ColoringRule) reads: color(a0) = color(a2) = β and color(a1) + color(a3) = 2β.

Isotopic.summaryHtml: The surprise: 'isotopic' here isn't derived from Reidemeister moves alone. It's a list of 25 rules (flypes, half-turns, inversions, transfer moves), each a classical fact taken as primitive. One may be stronger than real isotopy.
Isotopic.bodyHtml:
Plain English

Definition (Isotopic, Flype.lean lines 120-184). The smallest relation on diagrams that

  • is reflexive, symmetric and transitive;
  • contains every Reidemeister move and planar isotopy (ReidemeisterMove);
  • contains the assumed moves:
    • local flypes (IsLocalFlype) and the Figure 5 slides flype_slide_add/mul: [±1] + t ∼ t.rot180 + [±1];
    • congruences: isotopic pieces give isotopic sums, products, half-turns, inverses and mirrors;
    • identities: (T+S).rot180 ∼ S.rot180 + T.rot180, (T+S)ⁱ ∼ Sⁱ * Tⁱ, (T*S)ⁱ ∼ Tⁱ + Sⁱ, associativity, [0] + T ∼ T, [±1] ∼ [±1]ⁱ;
    • the transfer moves of Figure 14: (T + [−1]) * [+1] ∼ [+1] + (−T)ⁱ and its sign-switched twin.

These are classical facts about tangles, but in Lean they are generators, not theorems.

Is it too generous?

The Claude audit found one real risk. flype_slide_add uses a planar half-turn of any t (rot180). The classical flype uses a single flip t^h, and the half-turn is two flips. For rational t the two are isotopic (flipping lemma), so the move is fine there; every use I found is on a rational piece. For non-rational t it may not be an isotopy. Also, Isotopic never asks diagrams to be well-formed.

A too-generous Isotopic would make "same fraction ⇒ isotopic" weaker, not false.
caveatsHtml: flype_slide_add/mul and transfer_odd(_neg) are quantified over arbitrary diagrams; the first may exceed real isotopy for non-rational pieces (Claude audit, §5: 'unresolved risk, flagged').
No well-formedness or planarity is required anywhere in Isotopic.

TangleDiagram.add.summaryHtml: The surprise: gluing two tangles side by side is just list concatenation plus renaming: shift S's arc numbers past T's, then identify S's west ends with T's east ends.
TangleDiagram.add.bodyHtml:
Plain English

Definition (TangleDiagram.add, Tangle.lean lines 98-109). Place S to the right of T, joining T's NE to S's NW and T's SE to S's SW. In code:

  1. rename S's arcs by adding T's largest arc number + 1, so they don't clash;
  2. rename S's NW arc to T's NE arc and S's SW arc to T's SE arc;
  3. concatenate the crossing lists. The new corners are T's NW/SW and S's NE/SE.

Fractions add: F(T + S) = F(T) + F(S), for rational T and S whenever the sum is rational.

TangleDiagram.summaryHtml: The surprise: a tangle is stored as a list of crossings, each four arc numbers plus a sign, and the arc numbers at the four corners. No geometry at all, and nothing forces the code to be drawable in a disc.
TangleDiagram.bodyHtml:
Plain English

A 2-tangle is two strings in a ball with their four ends pinned at the corners NW, NE, SE, SW of the picture (plus possibly closed loops).

Definition (TangleDiagram, Reidemeister.lean lines 177-187). A diagram is

  • crossings: a list of Crossings. Each crossing names the four arcs that meet it, counterclockwise, with the over-strand on ports 0 and 2, plus a sign;
  • NW, NE, SE, SW: the arc number touching each corner.

This is the tangle version of a knot's PD code. It was chosen so an integer coloring is just a function from arc numbers to ℤ (IsColored).

The trivial tangles have no crossings: [0] (two horizontal arcs) and [∞] (two vertical arcs).
caveatsHtml: No planarity or well-formedness is built into the type (Claude audit, §5).

TwistExpr.fraction.summaryHtml: The surprise: the formula for a top product is off: it gives 1/(s + F) where the Conway product needs 1/(s + 1/F). That's why the classification headlines exclude top products.
TwistExpr.fraction.bodyHtml:
Plain English

Definition (TwistExpr.fraction, TangleFraction.lean lines 30-38). Evaluate the recipe in ℚ ∪ {∞} (CFValue):

  • [0] ↦ 0, [∞] ↦ ∞, [±1] ↦ ±1;
  • adding [s] on either side: F ↦ F + s;
  • multiplying [s] at the bottom: F ↦ 1/(1/F + s).

Worked example. Start at [0], add [+1] three times: 3. Multiply [+1] at the bottom: 1/(1/3 + 1) = 3/4. Add [+1]: 7/4.

The top product

The code says mulTop e s ↦ (s.cfValue.inv.add e.fraction).inv, that is 1/(1/s + F) = 1/(s + F). The Conway product [s] * T has 1/F = 1/s + 1/F(T), so the right value is 1/(s + 1/F). The two agree only when F = ±1. The repo knows this: its standard-form rewrite gives the right value (toStandard). The classification headlines assume noMulTop, where the formula is right.

Example: [+1] * [0] is a kink on top of two arcs and isotopes to [0], fraction 0. The formula gives 1/(1 + 0) = 1.
caveatsHtml: On recipes containing mulTop, this function is not the tangle fraction (Claude audit, §3). Headlines 1 and 2 assume noMulTop; headlines 3 and 4 use toStandard.fraction instead.

TwistExpr.slideReady.bodyHtml:
Plain English

Definition (TwistExpr.slideReady, ColoringToStandard.lean lines 72-76). Every addLeft step needs the inner diagram's NW and SW corners on different arcs. Every mulTop step needs its NW and NE on different arcs. Right additions and bottom products are unrestricted.

It is a two-line wrapper around coloring_fraction_eq_F, which also asks for the diagonal rule NW + SE = NE + SW (DiagonalSum). Plain English

Kauffman–Lambropoulou's Theorem 2. The fraction of a rational tangle is an isotopy invariant.

What this Lean theorem says (coloring_fraction_invariant_ColoringIsotopy, DiagonalSumGeneral.lean lines 368-375). Let e₁, e₂ be slideReady twist recipes whose diagrams are linked by coloring-safe moves (ColoringIsotopy) from e₁ to e₂. Then

  1. their standard-form fractions agree (toStandard, StandardExpr.fraction), and
  2. every coloring fraction of e₁'s diagram is a coloring fraction of e₂'s (HasColoringFraction).

Color every arc with an integer so that at each crossing the two under-arcs average to the over-arc (IsColored). Read the four boundary colors NW, NE, SW, SE (ColorMatrix.of). The coloring fraction is (NE − NW)/(NE − SE) (ColorMatrix.fraction).

  • A coloring can be carried across each coloring-safe move without changing the boundary colors (coloring_fraction_ColoringIsotopy).
  • On a twist diagram, every non-constant coloring has coloring fraction equal to the arithmetic fraction (coloring_fraction_eq_F_any_slideReady).

So: color e₁, carry the coloring across, and read the same number at e₂.

rational_classification_fragment.bodyHtml:
Plain English

Conway's theorem (1970). Two rational tangles are isotopic if and only if they have the same fraction.

What this Lean theorem says (rational_classification_fragment, DiagonalSumGeneral.lean lines 584-592). Take two twist recipes e₁ and e₂ (TwistExpr) such that

  1. neither recipe ever multiplies a crossing on top (noMulTop),
  2. both pass a port side-condition (slideReady), and
  3. the diagram of e₁ can be turned into the diagram of e₂ by coloring-safe moves (ColoringIsotopy): Reidemeister I–III in the forms the project handles, planar isotopy, local flypes and gluing congruences, applied in one direction.

Then

  • their fractions are equal (TwistExpr.fraction), and
  • their diagrams are Isotopic.

How to read it

Both conclusions hang off the same hypothesis 3. So this is the shape "coloring-safe moves ⇒ same fraction" (one half of Conway, on a smaller move set), with the other half ("same fraction ⇒ isotopic") applied straight afterwards. The two halves never meet in an "if and only if" for a single relation:

  • the invariance half is proved only along ColoringIsotopy;
  • the reconstruction half lands in Isotopic, which is bigger.

The second conjunct says little beyond the hypothesis. Every coloring-safe move except the local Reidemeister III model is literally a constructor of Isotopic too, so ColoringIsotopy ⇒ Isotopic is one missing bridging lemma away from free. The proof doesn't use that; it goes the long way, through canonical continued fractions (twist_same_fraction_isotopic_of_noMulTop).

The docstring is candid about all this: "Full Isotopic invariance in either direction is not claimed."

twist_same_fraction_isotopic_of_noMulTop.bodyHtml:
Plain English

Theorem (twist_same_fraction_isotopic_of_noMulTop, CanonicalFormUnique.lean lines 126-132). If two twist recipes e₁ and e₂ (TwistExpr) never multiply on top (noMulTop) and have the same fraction (TwistExpr.fraction), then their diagrams are Isotopic.

This is the "reconstruction" half of Conway's theorem (Kauffman–Lambropoulou's Theorem 3), stated for recipes rather than for tangles up to isotopy. It covers every fraction: every recipe built only by adding on the right and multiplying at the bottom (standard form) is top-product-free, and standard forms reach every value in ℚ ∪ {∞}.

The idea

  1. Rewrite each recipe in standard form (toStandard): all additions on the right, all multiplications at the bottom. Moving a crossing from the left to the right of a tangle is a flype. The diagram stays isotopic (TwistExpr.toStandard_isotopic).
  2. On top-product-free recipes, the standard form has the same fraction (fraction_eq_toStandard_of_noMulTop).
  3. A standard form is a continued fraction [a₁, …, aₙ]. Using transfer moves and Reidemeister cancellations, push it to the canonical continued fraction of its value: odd length, all terms the same sign (ArithmeticCF.IsCanonical).
  4. Each rational has exactly one canonical continued fraction (continued_fraction_canonical_unique). So the two canonical diagrams are the same PD-code, and the two original diagrams are isotopic through it.

The infinite fraction 1/0 is handled separately: both sides isotope to [∞].
